utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are in open session now. This is a hearing of a Prosecution application for an order for the production of documents, dated the 16th of April. We have the application before us. We bear in mind, of course, the Blaskic guidelines or criteria in the judgement of the Appeal Chamber of the 29th of October, 1997. The request is to issue a binding order to Croatia to produce the documents listed within an annex within 45 calendar days, and in the event of nondisclosure, to appear before the Trial Chamber to show cause. It's your application, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've very fully argued in the motion of the 16th of April --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- fully argued in the motion of the 16th of April, we know nothing of the intended response of the state of Croatia to the motion, and in those circumstances, it may be better if I add nothing now but reserve what may be of further assistance when I hear the response of Mr. Casey, unless there is anything that's troubling the Chamber at the moment. The material sought -- perhaps I should then just outline -- the material sought is plainly relevant for the reasons set out in the motion, both because of the clear evidence of close contacts between Zagreb and those intimately involved in the subject matter of our case, because of the need to prove international armed conflict, they are all dealt with by the request or the documents subject of the request, we would invite the Chamber to say, for example, from evidence of regular meetings in Zagreb, of which it's already heard at the highest level, that it's simply impossible to accept that such meetings weren't documented, and that the documents will plainly be of assistance to this Chamber and should be produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Casey?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Let me begin by saying Croatia has not filed a written answer to the Prosecutor's application; it was our understanding that this was Croatia's opportunity to respond, and so we have not responded hitherto. With respect to the application, Croatia does not believe that the OTP's application meets the requirements of the Appeals Chamber's 29 October, 1997, judgement, any more than its original July 24th, 1998, application did. Although this question requests seeks materials regarding certain named individuals, the requests themselves continue to seek materials identified only by category and not the specific relevant documents required by the Appeal Chamber's decision. Indeed, the very number of the OTP's requests is, in and of itself, astounding. When the 41 individual categories of documents demanded by the OTP are considered, with the 22 separate subject matter areas listed in attachment 1, each has 22 subparts, for a grand total of 902 individual requests, each one seeking all documents or records of various types in a particular category that may be in the possession of any agency of the Croatian government. This, in and of itself, renders the request unduly onerous and inconsistent with the law of the International Tribunal. In suggesting that the application meets the requirements for a binding order under Article 29(2), the OTP has taken a position fundamentally at odds with the language and spirit of the 29 October, 1997, judgement. The OTP continues to treat the International Tribunal's authority to issue biding orders as a general investigative tool. Is it not. The authority of the International Tribunal to issue binding orders to states, under Article 29(2), as explained by the Appeals Chamber in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: -- my apologies -- as explained by the Appeals Chamber in the 29 October, 1997, judgement is, as the Chamber explained, a novel and unique power. As the Chamber continued, under customary international law, states, as a matter of principle, cannot be ordered, either by other states or by international bodies. As an extraordinary power, one exercised in derogation of the ordinary rules of international law, the International Tribunal's authority to issue binding orders to states should be narrowly construed and in accordance with the Appeals Chamber's strict ruling. In this respect, and in determining the proper scope of the International Tribunal's authority under Article 29(2), reference to the power of national courts to order production of evidence from third parties, whether in civil or criminal cases, which in most jurisdictions is narrow in any case, are not particularly instructive. As the Appeals Chamber stated in its 29 October, 1997, judgement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Casey. Where are you reading from, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: My notes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I thought you had been referring to the Blaskic judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: The first quote that I mentioned is on page 17 of the judgement. That would be paragraph 26, in about the middle of the page. The second quotation, which I'm about to read, is at paragraph 23, which would be on page 14. As the Appeals Chamber stated in its 29 October 1997 judgement, the Appeals Chamber holds that domestic judicial views or approaches should be handled with the greatest caution at the international level, lest one should fail to make due allowance for the unique characteristics of international criminal proceedings. Specifically with respect to what the Appeals Chamber termed the domestic analogy between national courts and the International Tribunal, it noted that, and I quote, "International courts do not necessarily possess, vis-à-vis organs of sovereign states, the same powers which accrue to national courts in respect of the administrative, legislative and political organs of the state. Hence, the transposition onto the International Community of legal institutions, constructs or approaches prevailing in national law may be a source of great confusion and misapprehension." That is at paragraph 40 of the Blaskic judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: All this is related to subpoena, isn't it? All the reasoning is related to the question of subpoena.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: We are not subpoenaing Croatia, or we are not discussing the question of subpoenaing from Croatia. Have this in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As a matter of fact, the case, while it did quash a subpoena issued to Croatia, also set the boundaries of, quote/unquote, "binding orders" under Article 29(2), and so the Court's language here is fully applicable to binding orders as well as the original subpoena that was at issue in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: I think there is a confusion, really. You are confusing between the binding order, which is accepted, really, by this Chamber, and the question of subpoena. All what is said and what you will recall here, what you are citing is related to the question of subpoena. The distinction is very clear, either in the decision of the Court or in all the commentaries which were given, you know, from this date by the scholars, by the professors, in the international reviews and so on, and I think it really will not help our Chamber to return to this discussion which is now very known, a very known distinction, so really, really, in all the faculties of law, I can assure you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, with respect, I think the Appellate Chamber was speaking a little more broadly, and the question of whether, as a matter of ordinary international law, a state can be compelled, whether it be under the name of subpoena or under the name of binding order, I think the answer is that as an ordinary matter, states cannot be compelled to, frankly, do anything by other states, with the exception of some very narrow instances where you may have a Security Council resolution specifically requiring a state or actually requiring other states to compel a state to do something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) You're saying, Mr. Casey, that it is on the basis of the Security Council, which established this Tribunal, and in Article 29 it has the authority to order a state, and that this was accepted by this Tribunal. But subpoena, subpoena is a different decision. It means the transposition of the national and international law, and this was rejected by this Tribunal. Now, this distinction between these two things is quite clear, and the Tribunal is fully empowered to order and to request and bind a state to produce a certain number of documents. I do not think that this is at issue any longer, and we do not have to evoke -- we can go back to Chapter 7, but we are not discussing it here. This, what we are talking about, has been accepted generally as something that the Tribunal may do. The transposition of certain national issues to international law is a different matter, but I believe that to us, it's quite clear, and if you are not clear about these distinctions, then evidently something has to be done about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the point you're making. Croatia does not contest the authority of the International Tribunal to issue binding orders, as was decided in the Appellate Court's judgement. All I'm saying is that in making that addition, the Court carved out, based upon Article 29(2), an exception to the ordinary rule of international law, and therefore it should be narrowly construed. I'm not saying that the Court does not have the authority to issue binding orders. The purpose of Article 29(2) is not to permit the OTP to conduct a general investigation, seeking documents that might be useful to the OTP's work in this or other cases or that might contain relevant information. Rather, the International Tribunal's authority to issue --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will you please slow down?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: The International Tribunal's authority to issue binding orders, under Article 29(2), is a device whereby states may be compelled to produce specific documents that each are deemed relevant to the trial of the accused and that are limited in number. These criteria, as the Trial Chamber noted in its 22 January 1999 order to Croatia, are cumulative and mandatory. The OTP's 16 April 1999 application does not meet these criteria. Indeed, the OTP concedes that it cannot, and I quote, "cannot specify the precise nature, date, author, recipient, and content of each specific document." This, however, is precisely what the Appellate Court decision requires. Even where the title, date and author of a document are known, the specific document sought must still be identified. Here, the OTP cannot even identify the nature of the documents it seeks. In support of its request, the OTP relies upon the separate opinion of Judge Shahabuddeen in an order issued to Croatia on July 21st, 1998, in the Blaskic case. This reliance is misplaced. First, Judge Shahabuddeen's opinion was attached to an order that, by and large, did request specific --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, slow down. The interpreters do not have a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is a problem if you read. If someone is reading something, they are inclined to go much more quickly, and everything here has to be interpreted. It's also more difficult for those trying to follow if you go too quickly, Mr. Casey. So can you please limit yourself?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: I will endeavour to slow down. Many of the requests in that order could, in fact, fairly be characterised as categorical in nature. They were identified as members of a class, in Judge Shahabuddeen's words. However, that identification was specific enough so that the actual documents desired by the OTP could be separated from all the other materials in Croatia's archives that might contain evidence relevant to the Blaskic trial, and these were emphatically limited in number. For example, one such request in paragraph 3 of that order sought military information summaries for the Second Guards Brigade, the Thunderbolts, quote/unquote, "from 1st September 1993 to 31 October 1993 while serving in Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." This request clearly meets the 29 October 1997 judgement, even though it does not identify each document by title, date and author but rather identifies those documents as members of a class. The type of documents sought, a, quote, "military information summary", is identified, as are the particular military information summaries desired, those for the Second Guards Battalion. Such summaries are generally kept on a daily basis, as I understand it. The request is further limited by date, September 1st through October 31st of 1993, and place. Only summaries prepared while the particular unit was serving in Bosnia and Herzegovina were called for. At most, some 60 odd documents could have been responsive. This is the level of specificity Judge Shahabuddeen had before him in writing this opinion, suggesting that categorical requests could be made. This level of specificity is nowhere to be found in the OTP's 16 April 1999 application. It is true that Judge Shahabuddeen goes on in his opinion to suggest that, quote, "I do not see that a demand for hundreds of documents is mechanically excluded if identification by reference to a clearly-defined category is readily possible." In his view, requests should be limited based upon an assessment of whether the number of documents sought is oppressive rather than an automatic prohibition of requests totalling in the hundreds. It might well be that a type of specifically-identified document could easily be produced, even if hundreds of such individual documents existed. However, a request seeking scores of different kinds of documents, resulting in the production of hundreds or thousands of documents, clearly cannot. In any case, the Appeals Chamber's 29 October 1997 judgement, both in plain language and spirit, requires that requests must identify a limited number of documents, and this language must be accorded some meaning in the context it was written. To the extent that Judge Shahabuddeen's opinion would eliminate this requirement, interpreting it out of existence and transforming the Article 29(2) binding order into a general investigatory tool, it is at odds with the Appeals Chamber's unanimous 29 October judgement and with the governing rules of international law and cannot control. Turning to the actual requests in the 16 April 1997 application, the scope of these requests again is breathtaking. Altogether, as I mentioned, there are 902 separate requests, each demanding all documents in particular categories, a number of these categories repeat requests already rejected by the Trial Chamber. For instance, in the 24 July 1998 application, the Prosecutors sought all records of various sorts relating to five meetings between Croatia's President Tudjman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're going to refer to some specific matters. You don't, by any chance, have it in writing, do you, those which you say are repeating requests which have been rejected?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: I do not have it in -- I have a couple of examples. I do not have it completely written up. I would be pleased, certainly, to provide that to the Court, but I do not have it with me now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Refer us, then, to those that you say are repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Very well. For example, in category 9(d) of the original request, the Prosecutor sought -- or rather that is in request 9, the Prosecutor sought records of various sorts relating to five meetings between President Tudjman and, among others, Mate Boban in the city of Split on 5 November 1993, and that is category 9(d). Now the OTP wants all records again of various times of meetings between Mate Boban and President Tudjman over a nearly three-year period of time, addressing any of 22 subject areas, including, quote/unquote, "the war, conflict, or hostilities in or upon any territory or area of the former Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What number request is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: That is item 4 of the subject matter group, and the request is -- I'm sorry, it's D of the subject matter group and request 4 of the annex. Indeed, the inclusion of this subject matter area, supposedly a limiting factor, has, in fact, effectively eliminated any limiting factor contained in the other 21 subject matter categories referring to the conflict or hostilities in the former Yugoslavia. Croatia has not, of course, had the opportunity to review the OTP's relevance claims, but it is inherently incredible that each of the documents called for by this request could be deemed relevant to Mr. Kordic's trial. Similarly, in its original application, and this is category 1 of the original application, the OTP sought, among other things, orders, communications, plans, memoranda of understandings and directives from President Tudjman to Defence Minister Susak, or their representatives, directed to Mate Boban and his representatives from May 1st, 1992, to January 1st, 1994 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Sure. -- regarding five subject matters including, among others, the presence, use and deployment of HV military police and intelligence personnel in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that was subpart A, and under subparts B and C, the Prosecution requested documents relating to the military and political goals and objectives of the HV and HVO military police and intelligence forces in Central Bosnia, including the municipalities of Vitez, Busovaca, Foca and Kiseljak. In the April 16th application, the OTP has asked, and this would be subject matters F, G and H, when put together with request, I believe it is, 3 or -- yes, that would be actually requests 4, 5 and 6 and 7 through -- and 7 and 8, or, I'm sorry, no, 7 and then 10 and 11, requesting documents including orders, directives, correspondence and et cetera from President Tudjman or Minister Susak to Mate Boban during a three-year period the 1st of June, 1991, to 31 March 1994, dealing with the presence, use and deployment of Croatian government forces or personnel on or within the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that is subject matter F, or the military and political goals of Croatian government forces or Bosnian Croat forces within the whole territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that is in subject matters G and H. In fact, the OTP is not merely on a fishing expedition here, it is using drift nets. Of the 41 principle categories of documents requested by the OTP, only 13 involve materials sent or received or kept, perhaps, by officials of the Croatian government, materials most likely to be in the Croatian government's possession. The balance of the OTP's requests involve individuals who, at the relevant times, were not officials of Croatia but either of the Bosnian Croat entity or the HVO. Seeking these materials from Croatia is merely a shot in the dark. Indeed, these are precisely the kinds of material one would expect to find in the HVO or Herceg-Bosna archives, which, as I understand it, were indeed raided by the OTP in September of last year. If the OTP already has access to this material, it is entirely inappropriate to seek duplicates from Croatia. Could the OTP's request be made to meet the standards articulated by the Appeals Chamber? In its current form, no. Could a request that meets those standards be formulated? Of course. If, for the moment, we jettison the paraphernalia of discovery, the interminable definitions, the indicatings (sic), recordings, evidencings (sic) and discussings (sic), and focus on individual documents that the Court could perhaps deem relevant to the accuseds' trial, it is possible the OTP largely did just this in the 21 July 1998 order to which Judge Shahabuddeen's opinion was attached. But what the OTP is not entitled to do is use Article 29(2) as a means to obtain access to hundreds of categories of undefined documents in order to determine whether anything of use or interest may be found therein. That is what the OTP has again attempted to do in the 16 April 1999 order, and the Trial Chamber should accordingly reject that application. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Casey, have you exhaustively listed all those requests which you say are repeats and, more significantly, were disallowed originally by the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, those are the ones that struck me when I was preparing. I have not gone through every category to determine which are duplicated. As I said, I would be pleased to do that for the Court, if you wish, and submit something in writing to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it's a pity that you didn't, Mr. Casey, if you're going to rely on the point. It would have been much better to have handed us a document so that we had it before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm sorry, I should have thought of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll hear the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, there's a measure of repetition. Just to remind the Chamber of what it's probably already recollected, the categories excluded in respect of the earlier application were excluded, I think, on the grounds of relevance, and there was an application by us to reconsider, which was rejected as a matter of principle by the Chamber. We were out of time to deal with the matter on appeal. The matter was brought back to you in a new form, with absolutely nothing to stop that being done. The Chamber, in our respectful position, is in a position to consider it afresh on its merits. If one turns to attachment 1 of our application, which is the categorisation, as it is said, of topics, this in part responds to one of the earlier objections by the State of Croatia to an earlier formulation in the request, where it was said that the subject matter of any meeting or communication was so widely defined that it could relate either, I think, to lunch or possibly to traffic tickets, something to that effect. Seeing the theoretical strength of that argument, it seemed appropriate for us to attempt to define what is and what everybody knows is at issue here. Thus, attachment 1 identifies topics in a sensible and coherent way and hopes, by those topics, to cover the whole territory with which, as everybody knows, we are interested. And when I say "the territory," which, as everybody knows, is that in which we are interested, I'm saying no more than the obvious. The State of Croatia well knows -- and it's important to have this in mind, from the way this case has been presented from its opening and since -- what is said to be significant in the meetings and communications between Croatia and those in Bosnia. It has two absolutely fundamental significances: One, international armed conflict; two, the role, the function, the authority, the purpose, the intention of the defendants, but in particular of the defendant Kordic. It's not a difficult story to narrate or to understand, and accordingly, if the Chamber will be good enough to come back and look at five pages before where we set out the documents that are sought, it's perhaps helpful to put oneself in the mind of or in the position of those dealing with this matter in Croatia, knowing the case raised against them -- not against them; against Kordic, and the issues that concern them -- was Kordic here to take instructions, to take soundings, to be advised on the conduct of affairs in Bosnia? Supposing the answer is yes, the question would then be: "And where is that documented?" They will know. Let us look, therefore, at paragraph 4, which I think has been referred to by Mr. Casey -- or 3 -- sorry, 3 is better; I'm grateful to Mr. Scott. They will know whether communications with and between Kordic and Franjo Tudjman were dealt with by what could be described as orders, directives, correspondence, letters, notes, or reports, and they will also know that if we limit ourselves, for example, to letters or to orders, and that if something can be properly categorised as a directive or a plan or a message, then, as it were, we would have failed by our particularity. So we absolutely have to cast our description sufficiently wide to cover all the categories of material as it may be described. But the underlying issue is a simple one. There were communications, they inevitably were documented, and finding those documents, frankly, can't be that difficult to those who know that they were created. Describing them is inevitably more difficult for us, but the description we provide is not onerous in any sense and certainly doesn't lack sufficient specificity. Likewise, Number 4, where it says minutes, notes, records, audio recordings, photographs, video recordings of or related to meetings between Franjo Tudjman and Mate Boban, the same significance: What is going on as between these two parties that concern Mate Boban with his role in Bosnia, how are they recorded? Yes, they were recorded. We have to ensure that the words we use don't allow a record to slip between our definitions so that the party concerned, knowing full well what's at stake, is able to say, "No, they've used the word 'note' and 'record,' and this is a minute, so we won't provide it." As was explained in our application, the apparent number and length of the list of requests and its details boils down to a very much shorter and smaller real target area. It's done by a number of plainly relevant individuals. It's done by the combination of those individuals together, and it seeks records, that the state of Croatia will know how it describes, covering those issues. They are plainly relevant, and the request we have made falls fair and square within the requirements of the Blaskic order. Incidentally -- I'm grateful to Mr. Scott again -- in our response of August of last year, but I can just read it to you, there was this paragraph, paragraph 4 -- I'll read it slowly -- "The former chief of the Croatian army has recently confirmed that many if not all the documents which the Prosecutor has been seeking since the 15th of January, 1997, are in the archives of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia in Zagreb." In an article in the 27th of September, 1998, edition of the Croatian newspaper Slobodan Dalmacia concerning the recent execution of search warrants in Bosnia and Herzegovina looking for many of the same or similar documents or information, General Janko Bobetko is quoted as saying: "I can't understand why they are looking for documents in Herzegovina and Central Bosnia when all the documents are kept in the archives of the Ministry of Defence in the Republic of Croatia." And that, I think, just responds to the point suggested that we've raided documents elsewhere. I think what Mr. Casey was referring to was the execution of a search warrant that was lawfully authorised, and publicised as such, and there is no question of there being a search here for duplicates of documents already available. That would be a waste of everyone's time. If this material that we assert must exist in records as we have, we hope, succinctly but accurately described, if such material was already available to us, we wouldn't be seeking it elsewhere. It isn't, and it must be available there, and that's why we seek it. Mr. Scott has prepared, in relation to the possible arguments on relevance that have been, I think, touched on by Mr. Casey, a small bundle of exhibits, and if it can help further with the question of whether these documents are too broad for the categories, if there is any other issue on the question of repetition of our request, may he just present this small bundle of exhibits?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I could hand the usher several documents, I think there's four, so perhaps for the Court initially -- and I'm sorry if I didn't make enough initially -- but there's one for Mr. Casey, and there's a second bundle as well, so there are two bundles of four. Allow me to start, only in passing, with the first one, which is titled "Report," and I know we're in open session, Your Honour, and I'm not going to make any reference to the content of the document other than this: The representations of arguments made by Mr. Casey to this Court, to this Chamber, about the level of cooperation and assistance in the Blaskic Chamber, we could not possibly disagree with more strongly, and this document in particular will indicate some additional background to this Chamber on the true state of Croatia's cooperation with this Tribunal. And I'll leave it at that for the moment, but this position has gotten to the point where it is misleading to this Court for this Chamber not to have this information in front of it. As to the separate packet of exhibits, what I want to touch on very quickly is, in part, Mr. Casey's position that some of the material we asked for in our request might, on the surface, appear to be more likely found in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As I hope the court is beginning to understand more all the time -- and I'm sure it does, forgive me if I suggest otherwise, I'm sure the Court does understand -- it's the Prosecutor's position, and we believe the evidence shows now, and will ultimately show at the conclusion of trial, that there was a deep and indeed virtually incestuous relationship between the Bosnian Croats and the government of Croatia. On one day you hear from one group that the documents are in Croatia, and the next day, literally, representatives from the government of Croatia come here and tell you, "They're in the Federation." Well, they're somewhere. One group says they're in Croatia, and the next group says they're in the Bosnian Croat side of the Federation. We are therefore required to seek them from both places. As an example, the first document of the 22nd of February, 1993 -- this is simply as a sampling. This is a communication from an HVO commander to an HV officer -- the 4th Split Brigade is a regular Croatian army unit, an HV unit, stationed in Split -- concerning the death of an HV soldier, not on the borders of Croatia and Bosnia, but deep in Central Bosnia, in Gornji Vakuf, an area that is directly relevant to this case. This HV soldier was killed in fighting between, as this HVO officer says, the so-called Bosnia/Herzegovina army and the HVO, was wounded by a sniper bullet and ultimately died in fighting. This was an HVO soldier in Central Bosnia. The next document, dated the 16th of May, 1993, is a similar letter or communication from actually the same HVO officer, Mr. Tokic, also addressed to a regular Croatian army HV unit, the 2nd Brigade of the Croatian army, requesting to use "your officer," that is, your regular HV army, Croatian army officer, "Mate Kunkic, at our disposal in the zone of responsibility of our brigade." Where is that brigade? Where is Mr. Kunkic, an officer of the Croatian army, located? Gornji Vakuf, in Central Bosnia. The letter goes on, and I won't take the Court's time to read it, imploring the HV to leave this officer in Central Bosnia, for he has been of great service. For instance, at the last sentence of the next-to-last paragraph, Mr. Tokic makes this statement: "There is no need to say that since last April, in these areas, he" -- that is, Mr. Kunkic -- "and his Alpha Force unit have considerably assisted in the organisation of our headquarters and later in the brigade. This HV army officer has considerably assisted in Central Bosnia." Alpha Force was an HVO force in Central Bosnia, the evidence will show, and apparently under the command of an HV officer. Why, again, is -- why do we ask for documents, for instance -- one moment, Your Honour -- for instance, in paragraph 28 of our request, of our annex -- and I will give the Court a moment to find that, because it's important -- in terms of our annex of requested items, as an example, paragraph 28. The evidence will show, and I don't think there will be any bona fide dispute about this, Slobodan Praljak was the chief of staff, the senior officer of the HVO, throughout Herceg-Bosna in large parts of 1993. So Mr. Casey may say, well, why are we asking for these documents from Croatia? Wouldn't the Federation -- wouldn't the Bosnian Croat Bosnian side of the Federation, the very -- have these documents? Well, the evidence will show that Slobodan Praljak was in fact a professional HV army officer -- had been -- had been moved from the HV in Croatia to become the chief of staff of the HVO during most of 1993. And the one document, just simply as a sampling, that I've given the Court, dated the 6th of November, 1992, the next one in the packet, is, in fact, an order signed by Major-general Slobodan Praljak to all members of the HVO and BH army, dated the 6th of November, 1992. Now, what happens to this very same Mr. Praljak, that -- and I go to the last exhibit and finish with this, Your Honour -- the last exhibit in this packet, which is the one that was referred to earlier, now copied and provided to the Court -- an order from the Minister of Defence of the state of Croatia, Mr. Susak, dated the 21st of December, 1993. And who is it, who is it that Mr. Susak, the Minister of Defence of the state of Croatia, puts in charge of the archive for the Croatian Ministry of Defence? For the Croatian -- an archive, again, likely to have a tremendous number of directly relevant documents for this Court that this Court should be able to see, that this court should examine -- and who does he put in charge of this? Slobodan Praljak, the same general who had just, days before this order -- days before this order -- was in Bosnia, was the chief of staff of the HVO. That is the reason why we have to ask for these documents from the Federation and from Croatia, because, I'll be very blunt with the Court, we can't tell for sure which place they are. We think there are reasons to believe that they are in both places or in one place. But given the relationship between the Bosnian Croats and Croatia, it is constantly a shell game. You lift the shell, and where is the pea? And the only thing the Prosecutor can do is lift all the shells until we find it, and so this Court can consider the evidence. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Casey, if you want to comment on the material which the Prosecutor has put in, then you may do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, just a few words. To begin with, with respect to the report in the other Trial Chamber, I have stated that Croatia has indeed cooperated. I have never suggested that the Office of the Prosecutor is satisfied with that. Indeed, the Prosecutor, Justice Arbour, any time she can find a crowd, seems to assert that Croatia has not cooperated to her satisfaction. Croatia's position is that it is not required to cooperate to her satisfaction; it is required to carry out its obligations to the Security Council, and through that, to the international Tribunal. With respect to the documents that the Prosecution has provided with respect to their claims of relevance, I'm not going to try to analyse them, since this is the first time I've seen them. I'm not even quite sure whether that would be appropriate, since Croatia's interests in this matter do not include whether the Prosecutor can or cannot prove its case. Croatia, however, has stated before the other Trial Chamber that it was involved in Bosnia, that it did give help to the HVO. It has stated that a number of both officers and regular private soldiers who were serving in the HV, many of whom indeed had come from the Herzegovinian areas of Bosnia when the war began with Serbia to fight in the Republic of Croatia's forces, when that war spread to Bosnia returned there and fought for the HVO. Some of those individuals later returned to the HV, General Praljak, I believe, being an example of that. All of that is indeed documented in the materials given to the Blaskic Trial Chamber. The extent to which the Prosecutor wishes to argue how -- what implications these particular documents may have is really a matter more, I think, for the Defence as opposed to Croatia. However, with respect to the bearing these documents may have on the relevance of the requests that the Prosecutor has made, to some extent they suggest ways in which the Prosecutor's requests can be narrowed. If indeed the Prosecutor believes that it can show that there was a, quote/unquote, "international armed conflict" in Bosnia in accordance with the legal definition of that under international law, then, indeed, orders from Croatian regular army officers to the HVO could perhaps provide some evidence of that. That would be for the Court to determine. They may also not prove that, but it is at least conceivable that such evidence could be found in such orders. That being the case, it would seem incumbent upon the Prosecution to ask for orders from relevant HV officers to relevant HVO officers during the period of time in question, as opposed to trying to sweep in every piece of paper that may have passed between various individuals over a three-year period. In fact, if the Prosecution has before it a specific legal issue it is trying to prove, it is not all that difficult to figure out the kinds of materials it will need to prove it. Moreover, defining order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Remember the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: I am sorry. Defining order also ought not to be that difficult. An order is a written directive from one individual to another, requiring that some action be taken. There is obviously always a problem or always a perceived problem that if you don't say, you know, "all orders, directives, communications," you may miss something. But if, in fact, you're only looking for very specific things, which is, in fact, all they are entitled to, then it should be quite easy to craft a request along with specific definitions that will produce -- assuming they exist, and I can't represent that one way or the other obviously -- documents that may inform them of the situation as it existed in Bosnia. And one other point: Croatia does not maintain and I certainly did not mean to suggest that there is no archive in Croatia, either in the Ministry of Defence or elsewhere. Of course there are archives. I think the question before the Tribunal and, indeed, that has been before the Court now for two years or more is whether the Prosecutor is entitled to have free run in that archive just to see what might be there of interest to it. Of course, it is the position of Croatia that it is simply not entitled to that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Casey, I think one has to be careful not to construe the Blaskic judgment as proscribing requests in respect of categories of documents. What it proscribes is a request in respect of a broad category, and the mere fact that a particular request begins with the phrase "all documents," et cetera, does not by itself render that a broad category, because the request may go on to include what I might term sufficiently limiting factors by reference to names, places, and to other characteristics which would render the request sufficiently specific in terms of a category to meet the criterion set out in the Blaskic Chamber. So I merely want to say that you have to be careful not to misconstrue the Blaskic decision in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I agree. I believe it is possible to formulate a request that seeks specific documents beginning with the words "all documents" and even in a categorical nature. I think, in fact, that one example of that was found in the order that the Chamber issued in the Cerkez case that is now in appeal. In its papers on appeal, Croatia has made very clear that a number of those requests it believes do meet the standard. I don't have it before me, but as I recall, one of those requests asked for all orders, directives -- there was generalised language, appointing Mr. Cerkez a commander of a particular unit. Well, that request clearly meets the standards. The Prosecutor didn't know what the document is called appointing an individual to command a particular unit, is it a commission, is it a directive, is it an order, and so they properly described it in a categorical nature, and that clearly meets the standards of the October 29 decision. However, in interpreting the phrase "broad category" as used by the Court in that decision, it has to be interpreted in context, both in terms of the other requirements that the Court there established for binding orders as well as in the context of that litigation itself. When the Court wrote that you couldn't ask for broad categories, what it had before it were a series of broad categories that sought unlimited numbers of documents that were not specifically defined. It said that, "No, you have to limit the number of documents you are looking for and you cannot ask for broad categories." Because the Court didn't simply say, "Categories are forbidden," does not suggest, I would submit that, that any category is permissible, just so long as the Prosecutor can say, "Well, we can't really tell you, we don't know what documents, so give them all to us and then we'll decide what we need." That is not what rule the Court laid down there. This, the Prosecutor's current application, frankly, does not comport -- it requests, indeed, it requests broad categories. Indeed, in looking at it, the only one of these requests that perhaps comes close as a substantive matter, if not in form, I believe, is number 40, which searches or is asking for orders, resolutions, declarations, various things regarding the award of decorations or medals to Mr. Kordic. Now, presumably, they don't know what again the documents awarding such things are called, and so we can tell from that that what they want to know is were decorations awarded and how was that done, and it may well be possible to produce a limited number of documents with respect to that. I think you have a very hard time narrowing the other categories in that fashion. Thank you. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In the light of the submission made on behalf of Croatia, that there are matters in the new request which repeat matters which have already been the subject of an order, we wish, at the least, to consider whether that submission has merit or not. In order to do so, we require a list of those requests in the new application which it is alleged are a repetition of earlier requests. Mr. Casey should have provided that. He said that he's prepared to do so, and we shall order it. Seven days, if you please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could perhaps have a few more days. Substantive materials that we prepare have to be reviewed by the client in Zagreb, and that may take a few extra days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How many days are you asking for?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Perhaps a week from this coming Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ten days --

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- from today's date, the Prosecutor to have seven days to respond thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll comply with that. Can I just touch on one point that I ought to have dealt with earlier? The request that is made is couched in the present tense, "items in the possession of the party." I've already made the point, in the most general of terms, that the Chamber may always be interested in knowing what items are not only possessed but what have been possessed. It would be open for it to cast any order it ultimately makes to include what has existed. Indeed, there's this general problem that arises in these cases where materials are produced, for example, in the course of a defence, something that's been observed in the Blaskic case, and where the provenance of the documents isn't known. Sometimes I think it can be even helpful for a party such as Croatia, if any order is to be made, to be under a duty to provide material within categories if it comes into its possession subsequently, to provide an account of it. Sorry not to make this point earlier, but I was reminded of it in the course of the hearing and hadn't therefore thought of it before. One of the problems that can arise is if a party to a case, in the course of his defence, or a witness on behalf of defendant produces a document late, is asked, "Well, where did that come from," then it's very late to go on the chase of the potential parties, "Was it this date, was it that date, was it somebody's private election," and so on, and it would help a general enquiry if one potential source of such late discovered documents was on notice to provide any information of material coming to it after the time of a particular order. So what we've couched simply in the present tense is something that might conveniently and helpfully be expanded to take care of what has been in possession of the party and also to deal with what may come into possession of the party. I see Mr. Casey wants to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might respond to that just for a moment, I think that that, in fact, is the standard of discovery: Anything in your possession or that may come into your possession. I believe it is inconsistent with the Appellate Court judgement not provided for in Article 29(2). I think it however does point out that the nature of the Prosecution's business here is to conduct discovery and not to obtain a binding order consistent with the Appellate Court's decision. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn.
